fields.Front: What are encapsulation and de-encapsulation? Show the packet at each layer going down the stack at the source and back up at the destination.
fields.Back:
Encapsulation: each layer adds its own header to the payload received from the layer above.
application: [M] message; transport: [Ht | M] segment; network: [Hn | Ht | M] datagram; link: [Hl | Hn | Ht | M] frame; physical: bits on the wire.
De-encapsulation at the destination is the reverse: the link layer removes Hl and passes the datagram up, the network layer removes Hn and passes the segment up, the transport layer removes Ht and delivers M to the application.

fields.Front: What two kinds of fields does a packet have at every layer, and what typically goes in Ht, Hn and Hl?
fields.Back:
Header fields (added by that layer) and a payload field (normally the packet from the layer above).
Ht (transport): port numbers, error-detection bits.
Hn (network): source and destination IP addresses.
Hl (link): link-layer addresses, e.g., Ethernet (MAC) addresses.

fields.Front: Compare hosts, link-layer switches and routers: how many layers each implements and which header each examines.
fields.Back:
Host: all 5 layers (complexity at the edge).
Link-layer switch: layers 1-2 (physical, link); examines the link header Hl; never looks at IP addresses.
Router: layers 1-3 (physical, link, network); strips the frame, examines the network header Hn (destination IP) to forward, then adds a new Hl for the outgoing link.

fields.Front: Is encapsulation always a one-to-one nesting of message in segment in datagram in frame? What complications exist?
fields.Back:
No. A large application message may be split across several transport segments, and a segment across several network datagrams, which must be reassembled at the receiver.
Also, a datagram may be re-framed with different link headers on each hop (WiFi frame, then Ethernet frame).

fields.Text: Encapsulation at the source: transport adds header {{c1::Ht}} to make a {{c1::segment}}; network adds {{c1::Hn}} to make a {{c1::datagram}}; link adds {{c1::Hl}} to make a {{c1::frame}}.

A link-layer switch implements {{c1::2}} layers and examines header {{c1::Hl}}; a router implements {{c1::3}} layers and forwards using header {{c1::Hn}}, rewriting {{c1::Hl}} on each hop; a host implements all {{c1::5}} layers.
